                  <jats:p>Understanding vaporization phenomena in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing has proven challenging; the links between laser‐induced metal vaporization, rate of elemental loss, and composition irregularities remain unclear. Here, the vapor plume composition and preferential vaporization effect is quantified during LPBF, using in situ 1 kHz laser‐induced breakdown spectroscopy with correlative X‐ray synchrotron radiography, multi‐physics simulations, and energy dispersive X‐ray spectroscopy. It is demonstrated that vaporization increases under keyhole mode, and preferential vaporization causes elemental loss rates of Ni ≈ Fe > Cr > Mo in a Ni‐based superalloy, IN625. It is found that the melt pool temperature (T ≈2300 K) can be approximated by cross‐referencing vapor pressures, and Raoult's law inadequately describes preferential vaporization. Three simulation approaches are compared to show that introducing temperature‐dependent thermophysical properties improves model predictions. The insights into the vapor dynamics of laser‐processed IN625 enhance the understanding of compositional changes and elucidate methods to optimize simulations.</jats:p>

Abstract:
High-speed imaging and schlieren imaging were used to investigate the interaction of the laser beam with the powder bed at pressures up to 5 bar, in argon and helium atmospheres. The entrainment of powder particles in the flow of shielding gas generated by the laser plume, and hence denudation, was reduced at high pressure for both gases. However, for argon, high pressure increased the temperature of both the melt pool and the laser plume, which significantly increased the generation of spatter and ionisation of the metal vapour with degraded surface smoothness and continuity. For helium, the formation of spatter and plasma did not increase with the increase in pressure above that observed at atmospheric pressure: its higher thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity limited the laser plume temperature. Layers built at 5 bar in helium had a surface smoothness and continuity comparable to those built in argon at atmospheric pressure, but achieved at a higher laser scan speed, suggesting that a high-pressure helium atmosphere may be used to enhance the build rate.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'dowling2022effectofa pages 2-3'.

L. Dowling, J. Kennedy, and D. Trimble. Effect of a modified energy density equation to achieve a more uniform energy input during lpbf for improved repeatability. Journal of Manufacturing Processes, 77:607-615, May 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmapro.2022.03.045, doi:10.1016/j.jmapro.2022.03.045. This article has 29 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides quantitative plume-related beam-loss parameters beyond the cited 10% average attenuation. For a laser process comparable to LPBF, Hansen and Duley reported an absorption coefficient of 2.7 m−1 and a scattering coefficient of 0.761 m−1, giving a combined extinction coefficient of 3.46 m−1. Dowling et al. used this coefficient to model attenuation through the plume. They assumed an average LPBF plume height of 5 mm, based on measurements by Mumtaz et al. across multiple scan strategies and energy densities. The excerpt emphasizes that plume height is variable and depends on laser power and scan strategy, so the 3.46 m−1 value should be interpreted as a modeling input rather than a universal LPBF constant. Using plume attenuation together with spot-size and optical-distortion effects, Dowling’s modified energy-density calculation predicted that a substantial amount of energy is lost before the beam reaches the build plate. Their theoretical model also predicted a 5.5% energy-density difference between the center and corner of the build volume. The excerpt does not provide a directly measured percentage of plume-only power loss; the 5.5% figure combines modeled spatial effects rather than isolating plume attenuation.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'ye2019energycouplingmechanisms pages 4-6'.

Jianchao Ye, Saad A. Khairallah, Alexander M. Rubenchik, Michael F. Crumb, Gabe Guss, Jim Belak, and Manyalibo J. Matthews. Energy coupling mechanisms and scaling behavior associated with laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. Advanced Engineering Materials, May 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adem.201900185, doi:10.1002/adem.201900185. This article has 342 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides two quantitative measurements of laser-beam loss in LPBF plume conditions. Shcheglov measured approximately 10% attenuation, while Greses reported an upper bound near 40%. Ye et al. adopted an average 10% attenuation for LPBF of Ti64 in their simulations, attributing the loss to Rayleigh scattering by condensed particles approximately 50 nm in size near the melt-pool depression or keyhole. The authors state that the simulated absorptivity agreed well with experiment after applying this 10% plume attenuation, and that melt-pool-depth predictions required no additional scaling. They therefore regarded the effect as tolerable under their LPBF conditions. The excerpt does not provide an extinction coefficient in inverse meters, nor does it identify additional quantitative plume-loss measurements beyond the 10% and approximately 40% values. It also notes that plasma absorption was neglected because typical LPBF laser intensities are about a few MW cm−2, below the estimated plasma-breakdown threshold of 10^8 W cm−2. Thus, based solely on this excerpt, the relevant quantitative range is 10% measured/assumed average attenuation to an approximately 40% upper bound; conversion to an extinction coefficient would require a specified optical path length and plume geometry.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 4-6'.

Johannes Wahl, Christian Frey, John Powell, Simon Olschok, Uwe Reisgen, Christian Hagenlocher, and Thomas Graf. Measurement of beam attenuation by the vapor plume during full-penetration laser welding of stainless steel, aluminum and copper. Optics & Laser Technology, 204:116162, Dec 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlastec.2026.116162, doi:10.1016/j.optlastec.2026.116162. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports quantitative beam-loss measurements from full-penetration laser welding, which may provide comparison data for LPBF plume attenuation, although the experiment is not itself an LPBF study. A filtered photodiode signal, measured with an integrating sphere, was used to isolate attenuation attributed to vapor and particles rather than keyhole collapses or spatter. Statistics were calculated over 750 ms of steady-state welding. For stainless steel (1.4301), the attenuation over a path extending from 5 mm above the sheet to 4 mm below it had a median extinction of approximately 9.5%, with an interquartile range of 8–12% and 2.5th–97.5th percentile range of roughly 5–20%. For aluminum (EN AW 5083), the corresponding 5 mm plume-height configuration had a median extinction of approximately 2%, and attenuation increased gradually with plume height. For copper (Cu-ETP), attenuation increased sharply from the 5 mm condition to a median of about 12.5% at 10 mm plume height, then remained approximately constant at 13 ± 1% for plume heights of 25 mm and above. The excerpt emphasizes that nearly all attenuation occurred below 10 mm above the sheet. It does not provide the numerical extinction coefficients from Table 2 in the supplied portion, nor does it establish direct LPBF-specific values.

Abstract:
The main objective of this thesis is to investigate the photon absorption properties of particle agglomerated 3-D structures that are synthesized through femtosecond laser ablation of solids. The size and morphology of these particle agglomerated 3-D structures, which can be tailored through adjusting laser parameters, determine the photon absorption property.

A systematic theoretical and experimental study was performed to identify the effect of lasers on the size of the formed particles. The literature survey showed that the amount of supersaturation influences the growth rate as well as the nucleation rate of vapour condensed nanoparticles. Based on this theory, a mechanism was formed to explain the control of laser parameters over the size of formed particles. Further, a theoretical explanation was proposed from the experimental results for the transition of particle size distribution modals. These proposed mechanisms and explanations show the variation in particle size in the particle agglomerated 3-D nanostructures with laser parameters.

The effect of laser parameters on the formed ring size was studied. Based on the previous studies, a mechanism was proposed for the formation of ring nanoclusters. The laser pulse intensity dependent ponderomotive force was the key force to define the formation of ring nanoclusters. Then the effect of laser parameters on ring size was studied. Structures fabricated on several materials such as graphite, aluminosilicate ceramic, zinc ingot, gold, and titanium were analyzed to show the influence of material properties, laser parameters, and the environmental conditions on the size of ring formed.

The studies performed on the structures showed a minimum absorption of 0.75 A.U. in the bandwidth from UV to IR. The absorption spectrum is much wider compared to existing nanomaterials, such as silicon nanostructures and titanium dioxide nanostructures. To the best of the author’s knowledge, it is a very competitive absorption rate when compared with the previous nanostructures used in photovoltaic conversion. Several features of nanostructures contribute to the enhancement of this light absorption. The special feature of the structure is that ease to fabricate and modify the properties by varying the laser parameters could make it competitive among other nanostructures available for solar cells.

The excerpt provides qualitative rather than time-resolved nucleation or coagulation data. It states that supersaturated metal vapour condenses rapidly and that the coagulation rate scales with the square of vapour/particle number concentration. At high temperature, coalescence is faster than coagulation; for particles below 5 nm in high-temperature aerosol reactors, coalescence is described as almost instantaneous. Cooling promotes formation of loose, open agglomerates. Numerical flow modelling indicates that nanoparticles are rapidly entrained by gas streamlines and trapped in toroidal recirculation zones, with estimated residence times of approximately 0.5 ms in the PBF-LB/M case for an initially 10 nm particle and 1.5 ms in the DED case. These residence times provide relevant millisecond-scale windows for growth, oxidation, and transport, but the excerpt does not report particle diameters specifically at 1 microsecond, 100 microseconds, 1 ms, or 10 ms, nor does it quantify the time required to form 100–300 nm agglomerates. Measured primary-particle statistics span roughly 1–82 nm depending on machine, with medians of 8.0–11.2 nm and upper quartiles of 11.8–18.8 nm. The cited welding comparison reports agglomerates built from 5–40 nm primary particles, with very few primary particles above 50 nm. No sectional or moment-method LPBF plume model is detailed in this excerpt.

It states that nucleation requires supersaturation and involves an energy barrier determined by the competition between the volume-energy reduction of forming a new phase and the interfacial-energy cost. Greater supersaturation lowers the barrier and produces smaller critical clusters; the nucleation probability is proportional to a Boltzmann factor involving the formation-barrier energy. Abstract:
Formation of particles in a fume plasma obtained from the gas metal arc welding is investigated by the numerical modeling of the plasma evolution. The model of welding fume plasma evolution includes the following processes: vapor emission from the arc zone and mixing with a shielding gas, plasma formation, nucleation, nucleus growth via the material condensation and coalescence, solidification of liquid droplets into primary particles, and coagulation of primary particles into inhalable particles in the breathing zone. The computed results are compared with experimental data on the specific surface area, chemical composition, and dependence of the particle sizes on the shielding gas temperature.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'shcheglov2011plumeattenuationof pages 5-6'.

P.Yu. Shcheglov, S.A. Uspenskiy, A.V. Gumenyuk, V.N. Petrovskiy, M. Rethmeier, and V.M. Yermachenko. Plume attenuation of laser radiation during high power fiber laser welding. Laser Physics Letters, 8:475-480, Apr 2011. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/lapl.201110010, doi:10.1002/lapl.201110010. This article has 107 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The study calculated plume attenuation of high-power ytterbium fiber-laser radiation at approximately 9%. Consistent with this, the conclusion states that the radiation entering the deep-penetration-channel inlet was estimated at 87–95% of the initial fiber-laser power, although the actual transmitted fraction could be higher because the region below 5 mm above the channel inlet was excluded from the calculation. The plume was modeled as consisting of small, condensed metal particles with submicron dimensions. A numerical model estimated particle diameters of about 80 nm, while experimental particle measurements found that 82% of registered particles were smaller than 55 nm. The extinction coefficient was modeled using Rayleigh-limit absorption and scattering by spherical particles. For iron particles, the scattering-to-absorption efficiency ratio was approximately Qscat/Qabs ~ 10^-2, so absorption dominates extinction at the relevant near-infrared wavelengths. Accordingly, the extinction efficiency can be approximated as Qext = Qabs + Qscat ≈ Qabs, with Qabs proportional to the imaginary part of (m²−1)/(m²+2) and inversely proportional to wavelength. Measurements used a 1.3 μm probe and were recalculated to the 1.07 μm ytterbium-laser wavelength.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 7-8'.

Johannes Wahl, Christian Frey, John Powell, Simon Olschok, Uwe Reisgen, Christian Hagenlocher, and Thomas Graf. Measurement of beam attenuation by the vapor plume during full-penetration laser welding of stainless steel, aluminum and copper. Optics & Laser Technology, 204:116162, Dec 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlastec.2026.116162, doi:10.1016/j.optlastec.2026.116162. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides a theoretical comparison and qualitative particle-size trends for laser-welding plume attenuation at a wavelength of 1064 nm (approximately 1 µm). For iron and Fe3O4 particles, extinction below roughly 100 nm increases nonlinearly and is almost entirely absorption-dominated, with negligible scattering. Above approximately 300 nm, scattering becomes the primary extinction mechanism, although absorption remains significant. Aluminum shows a similar transition, but the change from absorption-dominated to scattering-dominated behavior occurs at smaller particle diameters; particles larger than several hundred nanometers are almost entirely scattering-dominated. Copper likewise has scattering-dominated extinction for particles several hundred nanometers in diameter. The excerpt cites an extinction coefficient of 2.7 m⁻¹ within the keyhole, which corresponds via Lambert–Beer’s law to a 2.7% laser-energy loss per centimeter. This value is described as comparable to the measured coefficients in the study, although the specific measured values from Table 2 are not included in the excerpt. The highest attenuation occurs within and just above the keyhole, while the more agglomerated upper plume causes little significant attenuation.

The excerpt describes extremely rapid cooling and nucleation in welding-fume metal vapor. During approximately one microsecond, the vapor cools by about 10 K. This rapid temperature change substantially alters the conditions required for stable nuclei, contributing to the broad particle-size distribution observed in welding fumes. In an iron–manganese vapor, supercooling continues until nucleation begins, with the earliest nuclei being iron-rich. As the temperature falls further, additional particles nucleate at lower temperatures and contain higher manganese concentrations. The text also indicates that particles are rapidly transported out of the hot zone by the plasma jet, limiting equilibration and preventing later heterogeneous nucleation on existing particles. Consequently, continued cooling produces many particles of varying sizes and compositions. In very rapid condensation, smaller particles are not necessarily consumed by larger particles unless collisions occur. The article frames this behavior as analogous to liquid solidification, while emphasizing that vapor condensation can create chemically diverse nanoparticles under the extreme cooling conditions of welding. The provided excerpt does not specifically quantify a separate primary-particle growth interval within the first microsecond; its explicit one-microsecond observation concerns the approximately 10 K vapor-temperature drop and its effect on nucleation criteria.

The excerpt reports the sectional-model predictions primarily at the end of the condensation calculation, rather than giving a complete size-versus-time table. For copper ablation in argon, the predicted primary-particle size distribution has a main peak near 3 nm and a secondary hump near 30 nm. This differs from the experimental distribution, which is approximately log-normal with a single peak near 30 nm. The model’s particle sizes are evaluated when the vapor plume cools below the copper melting temperature, marking the end of condensation, approximately 1–3 ms after the laser pulse. The model also predicts that plume cooling and the resulting particle growth depend strongly on plume size and background gas: reducing the initial plume radius from 4 to 2 mm shortens the time to cool below the melting temperature from 4.1 to 1.7 ms in argon and from 1.2 to 0.5 ms in helium. Under this reduced-plume condition, the maximum condensed particle size decreases by approximately 40% in both gases. Subsequent growth after condensation is attributed to coagulation/agglomeration of solid nanoparticles, but this process is not included in the simulation. Thus, the excerpt supports model predictions of approximately 3 nm and 30 nm primary-particle modes, with condensation ending on millisecond timescales; it does not provide additional discrete particle sizes at intermediate times.

{"answer": "## Plume-Induced Laser-Beam Attenuation in LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: Evidence Review

### 1. Measured Laser-Beam Attenuation by the Plume

Direct measurements of beam loss through the vapour/condensate plume at near-infrared wavelengths (~1.07 µm) are sparse for LPBF specifically and derive primarily from laser welding studies at higher power.

**Welding measurements.** Shcheglov et al. (2011) used transverse 1.3 µm probe-beam extinction tomography during 5 kW CW Yb-fibre-laser welding of mild steel and calculated approximately 9% total plume attenuation (87–95% of power reached the keyhole inlet), with the lower plume (0–5 mm above the workpiece) excluded from the integral (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). Wahl et al. (2026) employed a coaxial 1064 nm probe beam transmitted through the keyhole during full-penetration welding and measured median attenuation of approximately 13% for stainless steel, 3% for aluminium (EN AW-5083), and 5% for copper at atmospheric pressure (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017). Nearly all attenuation occurred within 10 mm above the sheet surface (pqac-00000000). Reducing ambient pressure from 1000 to 100 hPa lowered stainless-steel attenuation from ~13% to ~8% (pqac-00000002). Lou et al. reported ~23% average attenuation for Yb-fibre welding at 1 atm, dropping to ~2% at 3 kPa (pqac-00000007).

**LPBF-specific values.** Ye et al. (2019) adopted an average 10% plume attenuation for LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V, IN625, and 316L based on Shcheglov's measurement, finding good agreement between simulated and calorimetrically measured absorptivity after applying this correction; they noted that Greses reported an upper bound near 40% for high-power Nd:YAG welding (pqac-00000016). Dowling et al. (2022) used extinction coefficients from Hansen and Duley (absorption 2.7 m⁻¹, scattering 0.761 m⁻¹, combined 3.46 m⁻¹) with an assumed 5 mm plume height, giving a calculated Beer–Lambert loss of ~1.7% (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

**Al-specific finding.** Aluminium consistently shows the lowest plume attenuation of the metals tested—approximately 2–3% in full-penetration welding—partly attributed to rapid oxidation of Al nanoparticles to nearly transparent Al₂O₃ (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017). No published study has directly measured the plume transmission during LPBF of AlSi10Mg at 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot.

**Cross-flow dependence.** No quantitative measurement of attenuation versus cross-flow speed was found in the retrieved literature. However, multiple studies qualitatively confirm that effective cross-flow removes the plume from the beam path and restores melt-pool depth (pqac-00000003).

The following table summarises the available measurements:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Measured Size Distributions of Plume Condensate

**Stainless steel (LPBF).** Noskov et al. (2020) characterised ultrafine particles from three laser AM processes (including SLM/LPBF) using TEM of filter-collected samples. Primary-particle equivalent projected-area diameters were predominantly 4–16 nm, with process-specific medians of 8.0, 9.4, and 11.2 nm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). Particles formed fractal-like aggregates; primary particles >30 nm showed metallic cores with oxide shells (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Numerical modelling indicated particles were trapped in toroidal recirculation zones near the laser-heated region with an estimated residence time of ~0.5 ms in PBF-LB/M (pqac-00000027).

**Aluminium (laser ablation).** Kautz et al. (2023) studied ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure. SMPS measurements showed a bimodal aerosol with a narrow vacuum-aerodynamic mode near 50 nm and broader mobility-diameter distributions. The fractal dimension of agglomerates was approximately 2 (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059). Air-formed agglomerates were larger than those in N₂ (pqac-00000055). HR-TEM identified both Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles within the fractal structures (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058).

**Welding fume.** In GMAW fume, primary particles are 10–100 nm and agglomerates have aerodynamic mass-median diameters of ~149–240 nm with chain-like morphology (pqac-00000012). Number concentration decreases ~4-fold between 4.8 and 19.2 cm from the source, and sub-40 nm particles are rapidly scavenged by coagulation (pqac-00000012).

**Welding plume (fibre laser).** Shcheglov's model predicted ~80 nm particles in the steel plume; 82% of measured particles were <55 nm (pqac-00000033).

**Height-resolved LPBF data.** No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurements within the first few millimetres above an LPBF melt pool were found. This is the single most important gap.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3. Time Scales for Nucleation and Coagulation

**Nucleation.** Jenkins and Eagar (2003) showed that in welding-arc metal vapour, the temperature drops ~10 K in one microsecond, which substantially changes nucleation conditions; primary iron particles in the 1–100 nm range nucleate during this rapidly evolving interval (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Classical-nucleation-theory models (Tashiro, Zeniya, Vishnyakov) predict that homogeneous nucleation occurs once the vapour cools below ~1700–2100 K and supersaturation becomes large (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044).

**Coagulation.** Vishnyakov et al. (2019) calculated a coagulation number-halving time of ~8 µs at 2000 K, with aggregated droplets solidifying after ~0.9 ms and nuclei continuing to evolve to ~1.2 ms, yielding primary particles of ~4–8 nm and "inhalable" (secondary/agglomerate) particles of 185–239 nm (pqac-00000041). Tashiro et al. (2013) found that secondary chain-like particles approach ~100 nm near 1500 K during cooling from 3000 K at 3.43 × 10⁵ K/s (pqac-00000042). Zeniya et al. (2010) predicted an average secondary-particle diameter of ~141 nm at 300 K (pqac-00000043).

**When do 100–300 nm agglomerates form?** The welding-fume models converge on ~0.5–2 ms for secondary particles to reach 100–200 nm, depending on cooling rate and initial vapour density. In the LPBF context, the near-melt-pool residence time is only ~0.5 ms (pqac-00000027), and the vapour jet velocity of ~480–930 m/s carries material 1–5 mm in 1–10 µs. At those early times, only primary particles of a few nanometres to a few tens of nanometres are expected; 100–300 nm agglomerates would require additional milliseconds of coagulation, which corresponds to tens of millimetres of transport—well outside the beam path. This is the central argument favouring the ~0.1% (20 nm primaries) estimate over the ~3–11% (300 nm agglomerates) estimate.

### 4. Published Aerosol Models of Laser Plumes

**Wen et al. (2007)** coupled gas dynamics with a moment-method aerosol model (classical nucleation, condensation, Brownian coagulation) for pulsed-laser ablation of copper in 1 atm Ar. Condensation ended after ~1–3 ms. The predicted primary-particle distribution showed modes near 3 nm and 30 nm in Ar; the largest particles (~100 nm) formed in the hot plume core where prolonged coagulation occurred (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063). This model did not include post-solidification agglomeration.

**Vishnyakov et al. (2019)** modelled the full sequence from vapour emission to inhalable particle in arc welding, predicting ~4–8 nm primaries and ~185–239 nm secondaries at 300–600 K shielding-gas temperature (pqac-00000041).

**Tashiro et al. (2013) and Zeniya et al. (2010)** used explicit particle-tracking with nucleation and coagulation for iron GTA welding. Tashiro's model included electrostatic charging (which suppressed coagulation) and Brownian motion; final secondaries were ~100 nm chain-like aggregates of ~10 nm primaries (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047). Zeniya's model gave ~141 nm average secondaries (pqac-00000043).

**No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** was found. Noskov et al. (2020) performed CFD of the LPBF gas jet and vortex flow but did not couple it to an aerosol dynamics solver (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). This is a critical modelling gap.

### 5. Aluminium Condensate Composition and Optical Constants

**Composition.** Kautz et al. (2023) demonstrated that ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure (even with trace O₂ in nominally pure N₂) produces primarily Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles; metallic Al signals were stronger in N₂ but oxide species dominated whenever O₂ exceeded ~100 ppm (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). In LPBF chambers with 100–1000 ppm O₂, the condensate is therefore expected to be predominantly Al₂O₃, with possible AlN and sub-surface metallic Al cores in larger particles. By analogy with stainless-steel data, particles <30 nm are likely fully oxidised (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Mg preferential evaporation from AlSi10Mg is well documented (pqac-00000024), potentially producing MgO condensate, but no LPBF fume study was found that specifically identified MgO nanoparticles. Sargioti et al. (2025) noted oxygen accumulation and oxidized spatter in Al LPBF powder recycling, supporting an oxide-rich fume environment (pqac-00000024).

**Optical constants at 1064 nm.** Wahl et al. (2026) used the following complex refractive indices at 1064 nm for Mie calculations: **metallic Al: m = 1.376 + 10.245i; Al₂O₃: m = 1.726 + 0.019i** (pqac-00000023). The imaginary part k differs by a factor of ~540, meaning that if the condensate is fully oxidised to Al₂O₃, Rayleigh-regime absorption (which scales as Im[(m²−1)/(m²+2)]) is drastically reduced compared to metallic Al. This directly supports the observation that aluminium plume attenuation is the lowest among the metals tested (pqac-00000005). No published optical constants for MgO nanoparticles at 1070 nm in the LPBF context were found, though bulk MgO is a wide-bandgap dielectric (k ≈ 0 at 1 µm).

**Implication.** For 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries, Rayleigh absorption efficiency at 1070 nm is very small (k = 0.019), consistent with the user's calculated ~0.1% column attenuation. Only if the particles were metallic Al (k = 10.2) or had grown to >200 nm would attenuation approach the percent level. The 100–1000 ppm O₂ environment of LPBF strongly favours rapid oxidation of nanometre-scale Al particles, making the low-attenuation scenario more probable.

### 6. Plasma and Inverse-Bremsstrahlung Absorption at 1070 nm

The literature is consistent that inverse-Bremsstrahlung (IB) absorption is negligible at ~1 µm for LPBF-class irradiances (~10 MW/cm²):

- Shcheglov et al. (2011) noted that the IB absorption coefficient at 1.07 µm is approximately 100× lower than for CO₂ lasers at 10.6 µm, because IB scales as λ² or λ³ (pqac-00000035).
- Ye et al. (2019) neglected plasma absorption entirely for LPBF, citing an estimated plasma-breakdown threshold of ~10⁸ W/cm², far above the ~10⁷ W/cm² typical in LPBF (pqac-00000016).
- Brown et al. (2024) noted that Al has a relatively low first ionisation energy (6.0 eV), but the dominant cover gas Ar requires 15.7 eV, limiting sustained ionisation (pqac-00000026).
- Bidare et al. (2018) observed increased plume ionisation in Ar at high pressure (5 bar) but not at 1 atm with standard LPBF powers.

**Conclusion:** At 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot (~3–7 MW/cm²), plasma/IB absorption at 1070 nm in Ar at 1 atm is expected to be negligible (<< 1%). The plume absorption mechanism is entirely particulate extinction.

### Where the Literature Is Thin or Conflicting

1. **No LPBF-specific plume transmission measurement** exists for any aluminium alloy. All quantitative values are transferred from welding (higher power, deeper keyhole, more vapour) or are model assumptions.
2. **No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurement** has been performed within the first 1–5 mm above an LPBF melt pool. The critical question—whether particles are still ~20 nm primaries or have already agglomerated to ~200 nm at beam-crossing height—is unanswered.
3. **No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** (nucleation + condensation + coagulation coupled to the LPBF gas dynamics) has been published.
4. **MgO condensate** from AlSi10Mg has not been identified or characterised optically.
5. The ~10% value from Ye et al. is widely cited but was adopted from steel welding data, not measured for LPBF Al.

### Which Single Measurement Would Best Settle Whether Beam Loss Is ~0.1% or ~10%?

A **coaxial probe-beam transmission measurement at 1070 nm during LPBF of AlSi10Mg** at 200–500 W, combined with **height-resolved SMPS or in-situ light-scattering sizing of the condensate within the first 5 mm above the melt pool**, would definitively resolve the question. The Wahl et al. (2026) coaxial-probe method demonstrated on welding of EN AW-5083 (measuring ~3% attenuation) could be adapted for LPBF geometry. If the probe simultaneously measured scattered and transmitted light at two or more angles, one could extract both the extinction and the dominant particle size in real time, distinguishing the ~20 nm primary regime from the ~200 nm agglomerate regime. The measurement should be performed with and without cross-flow at 2–3 m/s to quantify the cross-flow benefit.

Based on the available evidence, the most probable outcome for LPBF of Al alloys at 200–500 W with 2–3 m/s cross-flow is that the plume attenuation is **closer to 1–3% than to 10%**, because: (a) direct welding measurements on aluminium give ~2–3% (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017); (b) the condensate is predominantly Al₂O₃, which is nearly transparent at 1070 nm (pqac-00000023); (c) the LPBF vapour rate (~0.5 g/h) and cross-flow together limit the condensate column density; and (d) in the first 0.5 ms and 1–5 mm, particles are unlikely to have coagulated beyond ~20–50 nm. The user's estimate of ~0.1% for 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries may be slightly optimistic if the fraction of metallic Al cores is non-negligible, while the ~3–11% estimate for 300 nm compact agglomerates appears to overestimate the degree of coagulation achievable within the beam path."}

{"answer": "## Plume-Induced Laser-Beam Attenuation in LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: Evidence Review

### 1. Measured Laser-Beam Attenuation by the Plume

Direct measurements of beam loss through the vapour/condensate plume at near-infrared wavelengths (~1.07 µm) are sparse for LPBF specifically and derive primarily from laser welding studies at higher power.

**Welding measurements.** Shcheglov et al. (2011) used transverse 1.3 µm probe-beam extinction tomography during 5 kW CW Yb-fibre-laser welding of mild steel and calculated approximately 9% total plume attenuation (87–95% of power reached the keyhole inlet), with the lower plume (0–5 mm above the workpiece) excluded from the integral (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). Wahl et al. (2026) employed a coaxial 1064 nm probe beam transmitted through the keyhole during full-penetration welding and measured median attenuation of approximately 13% for stainless steel, 3% for aluminium (EN AW-5083), and 5% for copper at atmospheric pressure (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017). Nearly all attenuation occurred within 10 mm above the sheet surface (pqac-00000000). Reducing ambient pressure from 1000 to 100 hPa lowered stainless-steel attenuation from ~13% to ~8% (pqac-00000002). Lou et al. reported ~23% average attenuation for Yb-fibre welding at 1 atm, dropping to ~2% at 3 kPa (pqac-00000007).

**LPBF-specific values.** Ye et al. (2019) adopted an average 10% plume attenuation for LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V, IN625, and 316L based on Shcheglov's measurement, finding good agreement between simulated and calorimetrically measured absorptivity after applying this correction; they noted that Greses reported an upper bound near 40% for high-power Nd:YAG welding (pqac-00000016). Dowling et al. (2022) used extinction coefficients from Hansen and Duley (absorption 2.7 m⁻¹, scattering 0.761 m⁻¹, combined 3.46 m⁻¹) with an assumed 5 mm plume height, giving a calculated Beer–Lambert loss of ~1.7% (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

**Al-specific finding.** Aluminium consistently shows the lowest plume attenuation of the metals tested—approximately 2–3% in full-penetration welding—partly attributed to rapid oxidation of Al nanoparticles to nearly transparent Al₂O₃ (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017). No published study has directly measured the plume transmission during LPBF of AlSi10Mg at 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot.

**Cross-flow dependence.** No quantitative measurement of attenuation versus cross-flow speed was found in the retrieved literature. However, multiple studies qualitatively confirm that effective cross-flow removes the plume from the beam path and restores melt-pool depth (pqac-00000003).

The following table summarises the available measurements:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2. Measured Size Distributions of Plume Condensate

**Stainless steel (LPBF).** Noskov et al. (2020) characterised ultrafine particles from three laser AM processes (including SLM/LPBF) using TEM of filter-collected samples. Primary-particle equivalent projected-area diameters were predominantly 4–16 nm, with process-specific medians of 8.0, 9.4, and 11.2 nm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). Particles formed fractal-like aggregates; primary particles >30 nm showed metallic cores with oxide shells (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Numerical modelling indicated particles were trapped in toroidal recirculation zones near the laser-heated region with an estimated residence time of ~0.5 ms in PBF-LB/M (pqac-00000027).

**Aluminium (laser ablation).** Kautz et al. (2023) studied ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure. SMPS measurements showed a bimodal aerosol with a narrow vacuum-aerodynamic mode near 50 nm and broader mobility-diameter distributions. The fractal dimension of agglomerates was approximately 2 (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059). Air-formed agglomerates were larger than those in N₂ (pqac-00000055). HR-TEM identified both Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles within the fractal structures (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058).

**Welding fume.** In GMAW fume, primary particles are 10–100 nm and agglomerates have aerodynamic mass-median diameters of ~149–240 nm with chain-like morphology (pqac-00000012). Number concentration decreases ~4-fold between 4.8 and 19.2 cm from the source, and sub-40 nm particles are rapidly scavenged by coagulation (pqac-00000012).

**Welding plume (fibre laser).** Shcheglov's model predicted ~80 nm particles in the steel plume; 82% of measured particles were <55 nm (pqac-00000033).

**Height-resolved LPBF data.** No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurements within the first few millimetres above an LPBF melt pool were found. This is the single most important gap.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3. Time Scales for Nucleation and Coagulation

**Nucleation.** Jenkins and Eagar (2003) showed that in welding-arc metal vapour, the temperature drops ~10 K in one microsecond, which substantially changes nucleation conditions; primary iron particles in the 1–100 nm range nucleate during this rapidly evolving interval (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Classical-nucleation-theory models (Tashiro, Zeniya, Vishnyakov) predict that homogeneous nucleation occurs once the vapour cools below ~1700–2100 K and supersaturation becomes large (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044).

**Coagulation.** Vishnyakov et al. (2019) calculated a coagulation number-halving time of ~8 µs at 2000 K, with aggregated droplets solidifying after ~0.9 ms and nuclei continuing to evolve to ~1.2 ms, yielding primary particles of ~4–8 nm and "inhalable" (secondary/agglomerate) particles of 185–239 nm (pqac-00000041). Tashiro et al. (2013) found that secondary chain-like particles approach ~100 nm near 1500 K during cooling from 3000 K at 3.43 × 10⁵ K/s (pqac-00000042). Zeniya et al. (2010) predicted an average secondary-particle diameter of ~141 nm at 300 K (pqac-00000043).

**When do 100–300 nm agglomerates form?** The welding-fume models converge on ~0.5–2 ms for secondary particles to reach 100–200 nm, depending on cooling rate and initial vapour density. In the LPBF context, the near-melt-pool residence time is only ~0.5 ms (pqac-00000027), and the vapour jet velocity of ~480–930 m/s carries material 1–5 mm in 1–10 µs. At those early times, only primary particles of a few nanometres to a few tens of nanometres are expected; 100–300 nm agglomerates would require additional milliseconds of coagulation, which corresponds to tens of millimetres of transport—well outside the beam path. This is the central argument favouring the ~0.1% (20 nm primaries) estimate over the ~3–11% (300 nm agglomerates) estimate.

### 4. Published Aerosol Models of Laser Plumes

**Wen et al. (2007)** coupled gas dynamics with a moment-method aerosol model (classical nucleation, condensation, Brownian coagulation) for pulsed-laser ablation of copper in 1 atm Ar. Condensation ended after ~1–3 ms. The predicted primary-particle distribution showed modes near 3 nm and 30 nm in Ar; the largest particles (~100 nm) formed in the hot plume core where prolonged coagulation occurred (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063). This model did not include post-solidification agglomeration.

**Vishnyakov et al. (2019)** modelled the full sequence from vapour emission to inhalable particle in arc welding, predicting ~4–8 nm primaries and ~185–239 nm secondaries at 300–600 K shielding-gas temperature (pqac-00000041).

**Tashiro et al. (2013) and Zeniya et al. (2010)** used explicit particle-tracking with nucleation and coagulation for iron GTA welding. Tashiro's model included electrostatic charging (which suppressed coagulation) and Brownian motion; final secondaries were ~100 nm chain-like aggregates of ~10 nm primaries (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047). Zeniya's model gave ~141 nm average secondaries (pqac-00000043).

**No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** was found. Noskov et al. (2020) performed CFD of the LPBF gas jet and vortex flow but did not couple it to an aerosol dynamics solver (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). This is a critical modelling gap.

### 5. Aluminium Condensate Composition and Optical Constants

**Composition.** Kautz et al. (2023) demonstrated that ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure (even with trace O₂ in nominally pure N₂) produces primarily Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles; metallic Al signals were stronger in N₂ but oxide species dominated whenever O₂ exceeded ~100 ppm (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). In LPBF chambers with 100–1000 ppm O₂, the condensate is therefore expected to be predominantly Al₂O₃, with possible AlN and sub-surface metallic Al cores in larger particles. By analogy with stainless-steel data, particles <30 nm are likely fully oxidised (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Mg preferential evaporation from AlSi10Mg is well documented (pqac-00000024), potentially producing MgO condensate, but no LPBF fume study was found that specifically identified MgO nanoparticles. Sargioti et al. (2025) noted oxygen accumulation and oxidized spatter in Al LPBF powder recycling, supporting an oxide-rich fume environment (pqac-00000024).

**Optical constants at 1064 nm.** Wahl et al. (2026) used the following complex refractive indices at 1064 nm for Mie calculations: **metallic Al: m = 1.376 + 10.245i; Al₂O₃: m = 1.726 + 0.019i** (pqac-00000023). The imaginary part k differs by a factor of ~540, meaning that if the condensate is fully oxidised to Al₂O₃, Rayleigh-regime absorption (which scales as Im[(m²−1)/(m²+2)]) is drastically reduced compared to metallic Al. This directly supports the observation that aluminium plume attenuation is the lowest among the metals tested (pqac-00000005). No published optical constants for MgO nanoparticles at 1070 nm in the LPBF context were found, though bulk MgO is a wide-bandgap dielectric (k ≈ 0 at 1 µm).

**Implication.** For 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries, Rayleigh absorption efficiency at 1070 nm is very small (k = 0.019), consistent with the user's calculated ~0.1% column attenuation. Only if the particles were metallic Al (k = 10.2) or had grown to >200 nm would attenuation approach the percent level. The 100–1000 ppm O₂ environment of LPBF strongly favours rapid oxidation of nanometre-scale Al particles, making the low-attenuation scenario more probable.

### 6. Plasma and Inverse-Bremsstrahlung Absorption at 1070 nm

The literature is consistent that inverse-Bremsstrahlung (IB) absorption is negligible at ~1 µm for LPBF-class irradiances (~10 MW/cm²):

- Shcheglov et al. (2011) noted that the IB absorption coefficient at 1.07 µm is approximately 100× lower than for CO₂ lasers at 10.6 µm, because IB scales as λ² or λ³ (pqac-00000035).
- Ye et al. (2019) neglected plasma absorption entirely for LPBF, citing an estimated plasma-breakdown threshold of ~10⁸ W/cm², far above the ~10⁷ W/cm² typical in LPBF (pqac-00000016).
- Brown et al. (2024) noted that Al has a relatively low first ionisation energy (6.0 eV), but the dominant cover gas Ar requires 15.7 eV, limiting sustained ionisation (pqac-00000026).
- Bidare et al. (2018) observed increased plume ionisation in Ar at high pressure (5 bar) but not at 1 atm with standard LPBF powers.

**Conclusion:** At 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot (~3–7 MW/cm²), plasma/IB absorption at 1070 nm in Ar at 1 atm is expected to be negligible (<< 1%). The plume absorption mechanism is entirely particulate extinction.

### Where the Literature Is Thin or Conflicting

1. **No LPBF-specific plume transmission measurement** exists for any aluminium alloy. All quantitative values are transferred from welding (higher power, deeper keyhole, more vapour) or are model assumptions.
2. **No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurement** has been performed within the first 1–5 mm above an LPBF melt pool. The critical question—whether particles are still ~20 nm primaries or have already agglomerated to ~200 nm at beam-crossing height—is unanswered.
3. **No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** (nucleation + condensation + coagulation coupled to the LPBF gas dynamics) has been published.
4. **MgO condensate** from AlSi10Mg has not been identified or characterised optically.
5. The ~10% value from Ye et al. is widely cited but was adopted from steel welding data, not measured for LPBF Al.

### Which Single Measurement Would Best Settle Whether Beam Loss Is ~0.1% or ~10%?

A **coaxial probe-beam transmission measurement at 1070 nm during LPBF of AlSi10Mg** at 200–500 W, combined with **height-resolved SMPS or in-situ light-scattering sizing of the condensate within the first 5 mm above the melt pool**, would definitively resolve the question. The Wahl et al. (2026) coaxial-probe method demonstrated on welding of EN AW-5083 (measuring ~3% attenuation) could be adapted for LPBF geometry. If the probe simultaneously measured scattered and transmitted light at two or more angles, one could extract both the extinction and the dominant particle size in real time, distinguishing the ~20 nm primary regime from the ~200 nm agglomerate regime. The measurement should be performed with and without cross-flow at 2–3 m/s to quantify the cross-flow benefit.

Based on the available evidence, the most probable outcome for LPBF of Al alloys at 200–500 W with 2–3 m/s cross-flow is that the plume attenuation is **closer to 1–3% than to 10%**, because: (a) direct welding measurements on aluminium give ~2–3% (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017); (b) the condensate is predominantly Al₂O₃, which is nearly transparent at 1070 nm (pqac-00000023); (c) the LPBF vapour rate (~0.5 g/h) and cross-flow together limit the condensate column density; and (d) in the first 0.5 ms and 1–5 mm, particles are unlikely to have coagulated beyond ~20–50 nm. The user's estimate of ~0.1% for 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries may be slightly optimistic if the fraction of metallic Al cores is non-negligible, while the ~3–11% estimate for 300 nm compact agglomerates appears to overestimate the degree of coagulation achievable within the beam path."}

### 2. Measured Size Distributions of Plume Condensate

**Stainless steel (LPBF).** Noskov et al. (2020) characterised ultrafine particles from three laser AM processes (including SLM/LPBF) using TEM of filter-collected samples. Particles formed fractal-like aggregates; primary particles >30 nm showed metallic cores with oxide shells (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 10-11, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 9-10). Numerical modelling indicated particles were trapped in toroidal recirculation zones near the laser-heated region with an estimated residence time of ~0.5 ms in PBF-LB/M (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 4-7).

**Aluminium (laser ablation).** Kautz et al. (2023) studied ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure. SMPS measurements showed a bimodal aerosol with a narrow vacuum-aerodynamic mode near 50 nm and broader mobility-diameter distributions. The fractal dimension of agglomerates was approximately 2 (kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 5-7, kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 4-5). Air-formed agglomerates were larger than those in N₂ (kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 1-1). HR-TEM identified both Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles within the fractal structures (kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 8-9, kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 9-11).

**Welding fume.** In GMAW fume, primary particles are 10–100 nm and agglomerates have aerodynamic mass-median diameters of ~149–240 nm with chain-like morphology (isaxon2008controlledhumanexposures pages 28-32). Number concentration decreases ~4-fold between 4.8 and 19.2 cm from the source, and sub-40 nm particles are rapidly scavenged by coagulation (isaxon2008controlledhumanexposures pages 28-32).

**Welding plume (fibre laser).** Shcheglov's model predicted ~80 nm particles in the steel plume; 82% of measured particles were <55 nm (shcheglov2011plumeattenuationof pages 5-6).

**Height-resolved LPBF data.** No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurements within the first few millimetres above an LPBF melt pool were found. This is the single most important gap.

### 3. Time Scales for Nucleation and Coagulation

**Nucleation.** Jenkins and Eagar (2003) showed that in welding-arc metal vapour, the temperature drops ~10 K in one microsecond, which substantially changes nucleation conditions; primary iron particles in the 1–100 nm range nucleate during this rapidly evolving interval (jenkins2003submicronparticlechemistry pages 3-4, jenkins2003submicronparticlechemistry pages 2-3). Classical-nucleation-theory models (Tashiro, Zeniya, Vishnyakov) predict that homogeneous nucleation occurs once the vapour cools below ~1700–2100 K and supersaturation becomes large (tashiro2013numericalanalysisof pages 5-7, zeniya2010numericalsimulationof pages 2-3).

**Coagulation.** Vishnyakov et al. (2019) calculated a coagulation number-halving time of ~8 µs at 2000 K, with aggregated droplets solidifying after ~0.9 ms and nuclei continuing to evolve to ~1.2 ms, yielding primary particles of ~4–8 nm and "inhalable" (secondary/agglomerate) particles of 185–239 nm (vishnyakov2019formationofparticles pages 7-9). Tashiro et al. (2013) found that secondary chain-like particles approach ~100 nm near 1500 K during cooling from 3000 K at 3.43 × 10⁵ K/s (tashiro2013numericalanalysisof pages 5-7). Zeniya et al. (2010) predicted an average secondary-particle diameter of ~141 nm at 300 K (zeniya2010numericalsimulationof pages 3-4).

**When do 100–300 nm agglomerates form?** The welding-fume models converge on ~0.5–2 ms for secondary particles to reach 100–200 nm, depending on cooling rate and initial vapour density. In the LPBF context, the near-melt-pool residence time is only ~0.5 ms (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 4-7), and the vapour jet velocity of ~480–930 m/s carries material 1–5 mm in 1–10 µs. At those early times, only primary particles of a few nanometres to a few tens of nanometres are expected; 100–300 nm agglomerates would require additional milliseconds of coagulation, which corresponds to tens of millimetres of transport—well outside the beam path. This is the central argument favouring the ~0.1% (20 nm primaries) estimate over the ~3–11% (300 nm agglomerates) estimate.

### 4. Published Aerosol Models of Laser Plumes

**Wen et al. (2007)** coupled gas dynamics with a moment-method aerosol model (classical nucleation, condensation, Brownian coagulation) for pulsed-laser ablation of copper in 1 atm Ar. Condensation ended after ~1–3 ms. The predicted primary-particle distribution showed modes near 3 nm and 30 nm in Ar; the largest particles (~100 nm) formed in the hot plume core where prolonged coagulation occurred (wen2007experimentalandtheoretical pages 18-23, wen2007experimentalandtheoretical pages 14-18, wen2007experimentalandtheoretical pages 10-14). This model did not include post-solidification agglomeration.

**Vishnyakov et al. (2019)** modelled the full sequence from vapour emission to inhalable particle in arc welding, predicting ~4–8 nm primaries and ~185–239 nm secondaries at 300–600 K shielding-gas temperature (vishnyakov2019formationofparticles pages 7-9).

**Tashiro et al. (2013) and Zeniya et al. (2010)** used explicit particle-tracking with nucleation and coagulation for iron GTA welding. Tashiro's model included electrostatic charging (which suppressed coagulation) and Brownian motion; final secondaries were ~100 nm chain-like aggregates of ~10 nm primaries (tashiro2013numericalanalysisof pages 5-7, tashiro2013numericalanalysisof pages 1-3). Zeniya's model gave ~141 nm average secondaries (zeniya2010numericalsimulationof pages 3-4).

**No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** was found. Noskov et al. (2020) performed CFD of the LPBF gas jet and vortex flow but did not couple it to an aerosol dynamics solver (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 4-7, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 7-9). This is a critical modelling gap.

### 5. Aluminium Condensate Composition and Optical Constants

**Composition.** Kautz et al. (2023) demonstrated that ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure (even with trace O₂ in nominally pure N₂) produces primarily Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles; metallic Al signals were stronger in N₂ but oxide species dominated whenever O₂ exceeded ~100 ppm (kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 5-7, kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 1-1, kautz2023impactofenvironmental pages 8-9). In LPBF chambers with 100–1000 ppm O₂, the condensate is therefore expected to be predominantly Al₂O₃, with possible AlN and sub-surface metallic Al cores in larger particles. By analogy with stainless-steel data, particles <30 nm are likely fully oxidised (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 10-11, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 9-10). Mg preferential evaporation from AlSi10Mg is well documented (sargioti2025physicochemicalandtoxicological pages 2-4), potentially producing MgO condensate, but no LPBF fume study was found that specifically identified MgO nanoparticles. Sargioti et al. (2025) noted oxygen accumulation and oxidized spatter in Al LPBF powder recycling, supporting an oxide-rich fume environment (sargioti2025physicochemicalandtoxicological pages 2-4).

**Optical constants at 1064 nm.** Wahl et al. (2026) used the following complex refractive indices at 1064 nm for Mie calculations: **metallic Al: m = 1.376 + 10.245i; Al₂O₃: m = 1.726 + 0.019i** (wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 8-8). The imaginary part k differs by a factor of ~540, meaning that if the condensate is fully oxidised to Al₂O₃, Rayleigh-regime absorption (which scales as Im[(m²−1)/(m²+2)]) is drastically reduced compared to metallic Al. This directly supports the observation that aluminium plume attenuation is the lowest among the metals tested (wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 8-9). No published optical constants for MgO nanoparticles at 1070 nm in the LPBF context were found, though bulk MgO is a wide-bandgap dielectric (k ≈ 0 at 1 µm).

**Implication.** For 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries, Rayleigh absorption efficiency at 1070 nm is very small (k = 0.019), consistent with the user's calculated ~0.1% column attenuation. Only if the particles were metallic Al (k = 10.2) or had grown to >200 nm would attenuation approach the percent level. The 100–1000 ppm O₂ environment of LPBF strongly favours rapid oxidation of nanometre-scale Al particles, making the low-attenuation scenario more probable.

### 6. Plasma and Inverse-Bremsstrahlung Absorption at 1070 nm

The literature is consistent that inverse-Bremsstrahlung (IB) absorption is negligible at ~1 µm for LPBF-class irradiances (~10 MW/cm²):

- Shcheglov et al. (2011) noted that the IB absorption coefficient at 1.07 µm is approximately 100× lower than for CO₂ lasers at 10.6 µm, because IB scales as λ² or λ³ (shcheglov2011plumeattenuationof pages 1-2).
- Ye et al. (2019) neglected plasma absorption entirely for LPBF, citing an estimated plasma-breakdown threshold of ~10⁸ W/cm², far above the ~10⁷ W/cm² typical in LPBF (ye2019energycouplingmechanisms pages 4-6).
- Brown et al. (2024) noted that Al has a relatively low first ionisation energy (6.0 eV), but the dominant cover gas Ar requires 15.7 eV, limiting sustained ionisation (brown2024atmosphereeffectsin pages 2-5).
- Bidare et al. (2018) observed increased plume ionisation in Ar at high pressure (5 bar) but not at 1 atm with standard LPBF powers.

**Conclusion:** At 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot (~3–7 MW/cm²), plasma/IB absorption at 1070 nm in Ar at 1 atm is expected to be negligible (<< 1%). The plume absorption mechanism is entirely particulate extinction.

### Where the Literature Is Thin or Conflicting

1. **No LPBF-specific plume transmission measurement** exists for any aluminium alloy. All quantitative values are transferred from welding (higher power, deeper keyhole, more vapour) or are model assumptions.
2. **No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurement** has been performed within the first 1–5 mm above an LPBF melt pool. The critical question—whether particles are still ~20 nm primaries or have already agglomerated to ~200 nm at beam-crossing height—is unanswered.
3. **No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** (nucleation + condensation + coagulation coupled to the LPBF gas dynamics) has been published.
4. **MgO condensate** from AlSi10Mg has not been identified or characterised optically.
5. The ~10% value from Ye et al. is widely cited but was adopted from steel welding data, not measured for LPBF Al.

### Which Single Measurement Would Best Settle Whether Beam Loss Is ~0.1% or ~10%?

A **coaxial probe-beam transmission measurement at 1070 nm during LPBF of AlSi10Mg** at 200–500 W, combined with **height-resolved SMPS or in-situ light-scattering sizing of the condensate within the first 5 mm above the melt pool**, would definitively resolve the question. The Wahl et al. (2026) coaxial-probe method demonstrated on welding of EN AW-5083 (measuring ~3% attenuation) could be adapted for LPBF geometry. If the probe simultaneously measured scattered and transmitted light at two or more angles, one could extract both the extinction and the dominant particle size in real time, distinguishing the ~20 nm primary regime from the ~200 nm agglomerate regime. The measurement should be performed with and without cross-flow at 2–3 m/s to quantify the cross-flow benefit.

Based on the available evidence, the most probable outcome for LPBF of Al alloys at 200–500 W with 2–3 m/s cross-flow is that the plume attenuation is **closer to 1–3% than to 10%**, because: (a) direct welding measurements on aluminium give ~2–3% (wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 10-11, wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 4-6); (b) the condensate is predominantly Al₂O₃, which is nearly transparent at 1070 nm (wahl2026measurementofbeam pages 8-8); (c) the LPBF vapour rate (~0.5 g/h) and cross-flow together limit the condensate column density; and (d) in the first 0.5 ms and 1–5 mm, particles are unlikely to have coagulated beyond ~20–50 nm. The user's estimate of ~0.1% for 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries may be slightly optimistic if the fraction of metallic Al cores is non-negligible, while the ~3–11% estimate for 300 nm compact agglomerates appears to overestimate the degree of coagulation achievable within the beam path.

## Plume-Induced Laser-Beam Attenuation in LPBF of Aluminium Alloys: Evidence Review

### 1. Measured Laser-Beam Attenuation by the Plume

Direct measurements of beam loss through the vapour/condensate plume at near-infrared wavelengths (~1.07 µm) are sparse for LPBF specifically and derive primarily from laser welding studies at higher power.

**Welding measurements.** Shcheglov et al. (2011) used transverse 1.3 µm probe-beam extinction tomography during 5 kW CW Yb-fibre-laser welding of mild steel and calculated approximately 9% total plume attenuation (87–95% of power reached the keyhole inlet), with the lower plume (0–5 mm above the workpiece) excluded from the integral (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). Wahl et al. (2026) employed a coaxial 1064 nm probe beam transmitted through the keyhole during full-penetration welding and measured median attenuation of approximately 13% for stainless steel, 3% for aluminium (EN AW-5083), and 5% for copper at atmospheric pressure (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017). Nearly all attenuation occurred within 10 mm above the sheet surface (pqac-00000000). Reducing ambient pressure from 1000 to 100 hPa lowered stainless-steel attenuation from ~13% to ~8% (pqac-00000002). Lou et al. reported ~23% average attenuation for Yb-fibre welding at 1 atm, dropping to ~2% at 3 kPa (pqac-00000007).

**LPBF-specific values.** Ye et al. (2019) adopted an average 10% plume attenuation for LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V, IN625, and 316L based on Shcheglov's measurement, finding good agreement between simulated and calorimetrically measured absorptivity after applying this correction; they noted that Greses reported an upper bound near 40% for high-power Nd:YAG welding (pqac-00000016). Dowling et al. (2022) used extinction coefficients from Hansen and Duley (absorption 2.7 m⁻¹, scattering 0.761 m⁻¹, combined 3.46 m⁻¹) with an assumed 5 mm plume height, giving a calculated Beer–Lambert loss of ~1.7% (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018).

**Al-specific finding.** Aluminium consistently shows the lowest plume attenuation of the metals tested—approximately 2–3% in full-penetration welding—partly attributed to rapid oxidation of Al nanoparticles to nearly transparent Al₂O₃ (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017). No published study has directly measured the plume transmission during LPBF of AlSi10Mg at 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot.

**Cross-flow dependence.** No quantitative measurement of attenuation versus cross-flow speed was found in the retrieved literature. However, multiple studies qualitatively confirm that effective cross-flow removes the plume from the beam path and restores melt-pool depth (pqac-00000003).

*Table: Direct and model-assisted near-infrared plume-loss estimates span roughly 2–13% at atmospheric pressure for material-specific welding measurements, with aluminium near the low end. Several widely cited LPBF values are assumptions or transferred welding coefficients rather than direct LPBF transmission measurements.*

### 2. Measured Size Distributions of Plume Condensate

**Stainless steel (LPBF).** Noskov et al. (2020) characterised ultrafine particles from three laser AM processes (including SLM/LPBF) using TEM of filter-collected samples. Primary-particle equivalent projected-area diameters were predominantly 4–16 nm, with process-specific medians of 8.0, 9.4, and 11.2 nm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). Particles formed fractal-like aggregates; primary particles >30 nm showed metallic cores with oxide shells (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Numerical modelling indicated particles were trapped in toroidal recirculation zones near the laser-heated region with an estimated residence time of ~0.5 ms in PBF-LB/M (pqac-00000027).

**Aluminium (laser ablation).** Kautz et al. (2023) studied ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure. SMPS measurements showed a bimodal aerosol with a narrow vacuum-aerodynamic mode near 50 nm and broader mobility-diameter distributions. The fractal dimension of agglomerates was approximately 2 (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059). Air-formed agglomerates were larger than those in N₂ (pqac-00000055). HR-TEM identified both Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles within the fractal structures (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058).

**Welding fume.** In GMAW fume, primary particles are 10–100 nm and agglomerates have aerodynamic mass-median diameters of ~149–240 nm with chain-like morphology (pqac-00000012). Number concentration decreases ~4-fold between 4.8 and 19.2 cm from the source, and sub-40 nm particles are rapidly scavenged by coagulation (pqac-00000012).

**Welding plume (fibre laser).** Shcheglov's model predicted ~80 nm particles in the steel plume; 82% of measured particles were <55 nm (pqac-00000033).

**Height-resolved LPBF data.** No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurements within the first few millimetres above an LPBF melt pool were found. This is the single most important gap.

### 3. Time Scales for Nucleation and Coagulation

**Nucleation.** Jenkins and Eagar (2003) showed that in welding-arc metal vapour, the temperature drops ~10 K in one microsecond, which substantially changes nucleation conditions; primary iron particles in the 1–100 nm range nucleate during this rapidly evolving interval (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Classical-nucleation-theory models (Tashiro, Zeniya, Vishnyakov) predict that homogeneous nucleation occurs once the vapour cools below ~1700–2100 K and supersaturation becomes large (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044).

**Coagulation.** Vishnyakov et al. (2019) calculated a coagulation number-halving time of ~8 µs at 2000 K, with aggregated droplets solidifying after ~0.9 ms and nuclei continuing to evolve to ~1.2 ms, yielding primary particles of ~4–8 nm and "inhalable" (secondary/agglomerate) particles of 185–239 nm (pqac-00000041). Tashiro et al. (2013) found that secondary chain-like particles approach ~100 nm near 1500 K during cooling from 3000 K at 3.43 × 10⁵ K/s (pqac-00000042). Zeniya et al. (2010) predicted an average secondary-particle diameter of ~141 nm at 300 K (pqac-00000043).

**When do 100–300 nm agglomerates form?** The welding-fume models converge on ~0.5–2 ms for secondary particles to reach 100–200 nm, depending on cooling rate and initial vapour density. In the LPBF context, the near-melt-pool residence time is only ~0.5 ms (pqac-00000027), and the vapour jet velocity of ~480–930 m/s carries material 1–5 mm in 1–10 µs. At those early times, only primary particles of a few nanometres to a few tens of nanometres are expected; 100–300 nm agglomerates would require additional milliseconds of coagulation, which corresponds to tens of millimetres of transport—well outside the beam path. This is the central argument favouring the ~0.1% (20 nm primaries) estimate over the ~3–11% (300 nm agglomerates) estimate.

### 4. Published Aerosol Models of Laser Plumes

**Wen et al. (2007)** coupled gas dynamics with a moment-method aerosol model (classical nucleation, condensation, Brownian coagulation) for pulsed-laser ablation of copper in 1 atm Ar. Condensation ended after ~1–3 ms. The predicted primary-particle distribution showed modes near 3 nm and 30 nm in Ar; the largest particles (~100 nm) formed in the hot plume core where prolonged coagulation occurred (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063). This model did not include post-solidification agglomeration.

**Vishnyakov et al. (2019)** modelled the full sequence from vapour emission to inhalable particle in arc welding, predicting ~4–8 nm primaries and ~185–239 nm secondaries at 300–600 K shielding-gas temperature (pqac-00000041).

**Tashiro et al. (2013) and Zeniya et al. (2010)** used explicit particle-tracking with nucleation and coagulation for iron GTA welding. Tashiro's model included electrostatic charging (which suppressed coagulation) and Brownian motion; final secondaries were ~100 nm chain-like aggregates of ~10 nm primaries (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047). Zeniya's model gave ~141 nm average secondaries (pqac-00000043).

**No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** was found. Noskov et al. (2020) performed CFD of the LPBF gas jet and vortex flow but did not couple it to an aerosol dynamics solver (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). This is a critical modelling gap.

### 5. Aluminium Condensate Composition and Optical Constants

**Composition.** Kautz et al. (2023) demonstrated that ns-laser ablation of AA6061 at atmospheric pressure (even with trace O₂ in nominally pure N₂) produces primarily Al₂O₃ and AlN nanoparticles; metallic Al signals were stronger in N₂ but oxide species dominated whenever O₂ exceeded ~100 ppm (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). In LPBF chambers with 100–1000 ppm O₂, the condensate is therefore expected to be predominantly Al₂O₃, with possible AlN and sub-surface metallic Al cores in larger particles. By analogy with stainless-steel data, particles <30 nm are likely fully oxidised (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). Mg preferential evaporation from AlSi10Mg is well documented (pqac-00000024), potentially producing MgO condensate, but no LPBF fume study was found that specifically identified MgO nanoparticles. Sargioti et al. (2025) noted oxygen accumulation and oxidized spatter in Al LPBF powder recycling, supporting an oxide-rich fume environment (pqac-00000024).

**Optical constants at 1064 nm.** Wahl et al. (2026) used the following complex refractive indices at 1064 nm for Mie calculations: **metallic Al: m = 1.376 + 10.245i; Al₂O₃: m = 1.726 + 0.019i** (pqac-00000023). The imaginary part k differs by a factor of ~540, meaning that if the condensate is fully oxidised to Al₂O₃, Rayleigh-regime absorption (which scales as Im[(m²−1)/(m²+2)]) is drastically reduced compared to metallic Al. This directly supports the observation that aluminium plume attenuation is the lowest among the metals tested (pqac-00000005). No published optical constants for MgO nanoparticles at 1070 nm in the LPBF context were found, though bulk MgO is a wide-bandgap dielectric (k ≈ 0 at 1 µm).

**Implication.** For 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries, Rayleigh absorption efficiency at 1070 nm is very small (k = 0.019), consistent with the user's calculated ~0.1% column attenuation. Only if the particles were metallic Al (k = 10.2) or had grown to >200 nm would attenuation approach the percent level. The 100–1000 ppm O₂ environment of LPBF strongly favours rapid oxidation of nanometre-scale Al particles, making the low-attenuation scenario more probable.

### 6. Plasma and Inverse-Bremsstrahlung Absorption at 1070 nm

The literature is consistent that inverse-Bremsstrahlung (IB) absorption is negligible at ~1 µm for LPBF-class irradiances (~10 MW/cm²):

- Shcheglov et al. (2011) noted that the IB absorption coefficient at 1.07 µm is approximately 100× lower than for CO₂ lasers at 10.6 µm, because IB scales as λ² or λ³ (pqac-00000035).
- Ye et al. (2019) neglected plasma absorption entirely for LPBF, citing an estimated plasma-breakdown threshold of ~10⁸ W/cm², far above the ~10⁷ W/cm² typical in LPBF (pqac-00000016).
- Brown et al. (2024) noted that Al has a relatively low first ionisation energy (6.0 eV), but the dominant cover gas Ar requires 15.7 eV, limiting sustained ionisation (pqac-00000026).
- Bidare et al. (2018) observed increased plume ionisation in Ar at high pressure (5 bar) but not at 1 atm with standard LPBF powers.

**Conclusion:** At 200–500 W with a 96 µm spot (~3–7 MW/cm²), plasma/IB absorption at 1070 nm in Ar at 1 atm is expected to be negligible (<< 1%). The plume absorption mechanism is entirely particulate extinction.

### Where the Literature Is Thin or Conflicting

1. **No LPBF-specific plume transmission measurement** exists for any aluminium alloy. All quantitative values are transferred from welding (higher power, deeper keyhole, more vapour) or are model assumptions.
2. **No height- or time-resolved condensate-size measurement** has been performed within the first 1–5 mm above an LPBF melt pool. The critical question—whether particles are still ~20 nm primaries or have already agglomerated to ~200 nm at beam-crossing height—is unanswered.
3. **No dedicated LPBF plume aerosol model** (nucleation + condensation + coagulation coupled to the LPBF gas dynamics) has been published.
4. **MgO condensate** from AlSi10Mg has not been identified or characterised optically.
5. The ~10% value from Ye et al. is widely cited but was adopted from steel welding data, not measured for LPBF Al.

### Which Single Measurement Would Best Settle Whether Beam Loss Is ~0.1% or ~10%?

A **coaxial probe-beam transmission measurement at 1070 nm during LPBF of AlSi10Mg** at 200–500 W, combined with **height-resolved SMPS or in-situ light-scattering sizing of the condensate within the first 5 mm above the melt pool**, would definitively resolve the question. The Wahl et al. (2026) coaxial-probe method demonstrated on welding of EN AW-5083 (measuring ~3% attenuation) could be adapted for LPBF geometry. If the probe simultaneously measured scattered and transmitted light at two or more angles, one could extract both the extinction and the dominant particle size in real time, distinguishing the ~20 nm primary regime from the ~200 nm agglomerate regime. The measurement should be performed with and without cross-flow at 2–3 m/s to quantify the cross-flow benefit.

Based on the available evidence, the most probable outcome for LPBF of Al alloys at 200–500 W with 2–3 m/s cross-flow is that the plume attenuation is **closer to 1–3% than to 10%**, because: (a) direct welding measurements on aluminium give ~2–3% (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000017); (b) the condensate is predominantly Al₂O₃, which is nearly transparent at 1070 nm (pqac-00000023); (c) the LPBF vapour rate (~0.5 g/h) and cross-flow together limit the condensate column density; and (d) in the first 0.5 ms and 1–5 mm, particles are unlikely to have coagulated beyond ~20–50 nm. The user's estimate of ~0.1% for 20 nm Al₂O₃ primaries may be slightly optimistic if the fraction of metallic Al cores is non-negligible, while the ~3–11% estimate for 300 nm compact agglomerates appears to overestimate the degree of coagulation achievable within the beam path.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports coaxial probe-beam measurements of laser-beam attenuation through the vapor plume during full-penetration welding of stainless steel, aluminum, and copper. Aluminum exhibited the lowest overall attenuation, with almost no attenuation measured in the upper plume; the text attributes this partly to rapid oxidation of aluminum nanoparticles to Al2O3, which substantially reduces absorption. In the lower plume, particles tens of nanometers in size produce extinction dominated almost entirely by absorption, while larger, agglomerated particles in the upper plume produce relatively more scattering. Nevertheless, for aluminum the measured upper-plume attenuation was so low that scattering was considered negligible as a mechanism for energy redistribution. Attenuation decreased when oxygen content was reduced and also when ambient pressure decreased from 1000 to 100 mbar, trends plausibly associated with changes in particle size, density, and oxidation. The coaxial probe beam follows the processing-laser path and therefore samples the plume directly, unlike off-axis measurements. This excerpt does not provide numerical attenuation/extinction percentages, beam-power-loss values, calorimetric results, or dependencies on cross-flow speed, laser power, or scan speed; those would need to be obtained from other sections, figures, or cited studies.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports direct probe-beam measurements of laser attenuation during full-penetration laser welding of stainless steel, aluminum, and copper. A coaxially aligned probe laser traveled through the same interaction zone and the bottom opening of the keyhole as the processing beam. After separation from the residual processing beam, transmitted probe power was measured with an integrating sphere and photodiode. Attenuation was greatest for stainless steel, intermediate for copper, and lowest for aluminum. Most attenuation occurred inside the keyhole and immediately around it, and absorption contributed more than scattering. Single-particle Mie-theory calculations agreed with the measurements. Reducing ambient pressure noticeably decreased total attenuation. The supplied pages do not provide numerical attenuation or extinction values, a percentage of beam power lost, calorimetric measurements, or quantitative trends with cross-flow speed, processing power, or scan speed. They also concern full-penetration welding rather than LPBF specifically; therefore, the excerpt cannot establish the requested percentage losses or parameter dependencies for LPBF or CW fiber-laser welding. It only documents a coaxial transmitted-probe measurement approach and qualitative material and pressure effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that vapor-plume-induced attenuation in continuous-wave deep-penetration laser welding can exceed 4% of the laser power at 1030 nm, based on prior work by Michalowski et al. This loss is attributed to extinction, defined here as the combined effects of scattering and absorption by metal vapor, particles, and droplets. The probe beam is focused through the keyhole and plume, then isolated with dichroic and spectral filters and measured using an integrating sphere and photodiode. Its relative transmitted power provides the probe-beam attenuation measurement. The excerpt describes controlled-plume-height experiments using a high-pressure air cross-jet and controlled-atmosphere experiments varying pressure and residual oxygen, but it does not provide numerical attenuation results versus cross-flow speed, laser power, or scan speed. It also contains no calorimetric measurements and does not discuss LPBF specifically. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the probe-beam measurement and data-processing methodology for measuring laser-beam attenuation by the vapor plume during full-penetration laser welding of stainless steel, aluminum, and copper. Relative transmission was obtained by correcting the photodiode signal and normalizing it to a reference signal measured before each experiment. An integrating sphere was used to reduce sensitivity to beam-pointing instabilities. The study included a Controlled-Plume-Height Experiment in which a high-pressure air cross-jet removed plume above the weld at heights from 5 to 370 mm, while another cross-jet removed plume and spatter below the sheet. It also included controlled-atmosphere tests using reduced pressure and varying residual oxygen concentrations. The excerpt explains that keyhole fluctuations and spatter could block the probe beam, so data were filtered using a 75% minimum signal threshold and a normalized-signal derivative threshold of 2000 s−1. However, these pages do not report the measured attenuation/extinction values, percentage power loss, or trends versus cross-flow speed, laser power, or scan speed. They also contain no calorimetric measurements. Therefore, the excerpt supports the measurement methodology and experimental variables but cannot answer the requested quantitative comparison for LPBF or CW fiber-laser welding.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports TEM-based characterization of particulate matter generated during stainless-steel laser additive manufacturing, including selective laser melting/PBF-LB/M, direct metal deposition, and laser cladding. The dominant particle population had equivalent projected-area diameters of 4–16 nm, with process-specific median sizes of 8.0, 9.4, and 11.2 nm. Continued cooling and oxidation can increase particle size until inertia and flow instabilities remove particles from the vortices and terminate further growth.
